title: When an AI Company Promises a Medical Miracle
hook: Midjourney, famous for AI art, now pitches a spa-like water tank that scans your body 'as powerful as an MRI' — but The Verge says the bold claims lack the evidence to back them.
key_points: Midjourney, best known for its AI image generator, announced a pivot into medical imaging.
Its pitch: an ultrasound body scanner that immerses you in water, 'as casual as a trip to the spa.'
It claims results 'as powerful as MRI' — an extraordinary promise for ultrasound.
The Verge reports the medical claims currently lack supporting evidence.
A follow-up behind-the-scenes video showed more of the 'dunk-tank' scanner design — but still no real proof it works.
Lesson: extraordinary AI health claims need extraordinary proof before you trust them.
content_html: When a company famous for one kind of AI suddenly promises a breakthrough in another, it's worth a careful look. The Verge reports that Midjourney — best known for generating images from text — announced a pivot into medical imaging: a futuristic ultrasound scanner that would immerse you in a tank of water and, the company hopes, produce "something as powerful as MRI" while being "as casual as a trip to the spa."
extra_html:
That's a striking promise. MRI and ultrasound are different technologies with very different strengths, and matching MRI-level imaging with a spa-like ultrasound would be a genuine leap. The trouble, as The Verge lays out, is that the claims so far aren't backed by published evidence. This is a textbook case of why AI health claims deserve extra skepticism: the stakes are high, the marketing is glossy, and an impressive demo or a confident announcement is not the same as data showing the thing actually works. For anyone reading AI health headlines, the useful filter is simple — ask what's been demonstrated, by whom, and reviewed by which independent experts, before treating a bold claim as fact.

A few weeks later, Midjourney released a nearly 20-minute behind-the-scenes video of the scanner — a "dunk-tank" design it hopes to deploy in spa-like settings for cheap, detailed, radiation-free imaging. The Verge's follow-up found the tour added more hardware detail but still left the core question unanswered: no published data showing the device actually delivers the imaging quality Midjourney claims. A glossier video is still not evidence — the same filter from before still applies.

related.title: Hype or Real?
related.hook: AI coverage swings between 'this changes everything' and 'it's all a bubble.' The truth is usually in between — and a few questions help you judge any big AI claim for yourself.

related.title: AI in Healthcare
related.hook: AI can spot a tumor on a scan faster than a tired radiologist and flag patterns no one would catch by eye. It's a powerful assistant to doctors — not a replacement for one.

choices.text: Its bold claims aren't yet backed by published evidence
Ultrasound is illegal to use on humans
Midjourney has never made any AI products before

flashcards.explanation_html: A glossy announcement and an impressive concept aren't the same as data showing the device actually works — which is what The Verge found missing.

flashcards.prompt: What's a good filter for any bold AI health claim?
flashcards.back_html: Ask what's actually been demonstrated, by whom, and whether independent experts have reviewed it — before treating the claim as fact.

flashcards.prompt: Why is matching 'MRI-level' imaging with ultrasound a big deal?
flashcards.back_html: They're different technologies with different strengths; getting MRI-quality results from a casual ultrasound would be a genuine leap — which is why it needs strong proof.

flashcards.prompt: Did Midjourney's follow-up behind-the-scenes video resolve the skepticism?
flashcards.back_html: No. The Verge's nearly 20-minute tour of the water-tank scanner showed more of the hardware but still no published evidence the device actually delivers MRI-level results.
